I made the mistake of HECKLING Henry Kissinger in the 70’s at the UN. He was giving a speech concerning his approach to Soviet détente, but I thought he was doing a stand-up routine about borscht.  This had less to do with his oration and more to do with the fact that, at the time, I was subsisting almost entirely on a diet of lithium and LSD. My memory is hazy as to what I was doing at the General Assembly Building, or how I even managed to get in, but at one point I called out from the gallery, “Yo Hank, why don’t you put a sock in it and get those legs shaved for once!”  Well, you can imagine this didn’t sit well with the dignitaries, and I’m sure the translators struggled to make sense of it as well, but nothing could have prepared me for what happened next. Kissinger stopped speaking and slowly raised his head, looking straight at me from across the auditorium. He began quivering with an intense scowl, to the point that his face began to turn blue in color and foam began to ooze from his grimace. This grotesque display went on for a good 45 minutes before he levitated above the assembly and flew directly over my head, still looking down into my eyes, and shaking violently as ever. It was at this point that the interior of the room turned into a kind of hellscape inferno and smoke began to billow from Kissinger’s ears. I have no idea what happened after that, but the next thing I knew I was lying half naked under the 59th St. bridge, covered in talcum powder.

Today's theme (and Munster Mike's pun) reminded me of a very interesting recent New Yorker story, What Would It Mean To See a New Color? (Olo can be described as the “greenest green,” though it can never be captured by a camera. But its development tells us a lot about our color vision.) "Ng’s hypothesis was that, if retinal cells were stimulated in ways that don’t occur naturally, “the set of perceivable colors” would be “significantly larger than the natural gamut of the human eye.” " https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/08/03/what-would-it-mean-to-see-a-new-color This resonated with me because once, on 4g of psilocybin, I closed my eyes for a spell and was zooming through space, and I saw a new color. I opened my eyes and exclaimed to my friends, "I just invented a new color!" And after a pause, "Wait, I can't do that!" My hypothesis is that 4g of shrooms unnaturally stimulated my retinal cells and that I did indeed see a new color.

This was a fun, quick solve, but I must admit I cringed at 65A. The account of Sojourner Truth's speech from which "ain't I a woman" is taken was published over a decade after the fact, and is written in a dialect that Sojourner herself did not speak. Contemporary reports recount a very different script. 

Imagine someone quoting JFK as having said, "We gon git ourselves up to that there moon in the next ten years or so, and a whole lot more besides, not on account of how it's like shooting fish in a barrel, but on account of how it's like herding cats." It's just straight up not what he said. Likewise, Sojourner Truth, who grew up in New York, did not speak in an exaggerated Southern accent. Her speech is well worth quoting, but only if you're going to use the words she actually said. The relevant line is "I am a woman's rights," which seems to me like a much more powerful quote anyhow.

Maybe it's because the cross-entries were easy, but I was surprised to see ATP in a Tuesday puzzle.  I remembered that from a college biochemistry course; that makes it a pretty specialized term.

Nice that, aside from the theme answers, there is no hint of green in the non-theme answers.  There are also lovely non-theme answers in the box – GLOSSES, PEDESTAL, HECKLER, ATELIER, and ENSHRINE.

My biggest jawdrop came when, post-solve, I learned that the everyday word JUNGLE has never appeared in the 80+ years of the NYT puzzle.  Sure, it has the letter J, but still.  Amazing! 

It’s a tough build, with much constriction, having every perimeter word be a theme answer, plus a revealer in the middle, and still end up with hardly a whiff of junk in the grid.  Impressive, even if this were not a debut puzzle.

Clever of Sunny to see a word we see all the time – WALGREENS – and rather than just move on, see not only a crossword theme, but this clever one.  

Bravo on that, Sunny, congratulations on your NYT debut, and thank you for a fun and zippy outing!

I just read the Wikipedia article on nitroglycerin, and it was fascinating.  I realize this was not really a part of the puzzle--trinitrotoluene was--but it sparked my curiosity.

I was reminded that it was a medication used for heart problems such as angina.

I was also reminded that it decomposes into carbon dioxide, elemental nitrogen, elemental oxygen, and water.  Assuming the water is also a gas at the conditions of detonation, there is no residue from pure nitroglycerin--it all converts to gases which are released at a velocity of nearly eight kilometers per *second*, which is 5 miles per second or 5x3600 = 18,000 miles per hour.  What a blast.  For space fans, that speed is orbital velocity on earth.

But I also learned that it's addictive!  Workers in nitroglycerin manufacturing develop and dependence on it, and withdrawal can be quite severe, even fatal.

Amazing chemical.

One more puzzle find. Just an amazing feat of construction. A Sunday from November 21, 1993 by Peter Gordon with the title: "Spectral Analysis." Fourteen rebus squares in that one, every one of them a color. Some examples: (YELLOW)SEA crossing (YELLOW)PAGES AL(GREEN) crossing (GREEN)BEANS ACLOCKWORK(ORANGE) crossing AGENT(ORANGE) SHRINKING(VIOLETS) and THE(BLUES) crossing... ...(VIOLETS)ARE(BLUE) ETHEL(RED) crossing SH(RED) And then the across answer in the very center of the puzzle: "After shower scene." (RED)(ORANGE)(INDIGO)(GREEN)(BLUE)(INDIGO)(VIOLET) think... ROYGBIV And some down crosses on that one: SYDNEY(GREEN)STREET (RED)ALERT (YELLOW)ER GO(BLUE) MOOD(INDIGO) ULTRA(VIOLET) Wow. Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=11/21/1993&h=72a ...

When you go into a pharmacy in Europe, you generally are in a two-aisle store where the focus is on medicine and other health-related items, with some cosmetics and general merchandise.  My grandfather had a store like that in NYC back in the day, and it was much like that, with the addition of a soda fountain. 

Large chain drugstores came into the scene that were larger, with triple the floor space or more, and a greater variety of items. They put many of the smaller pharmacies out of business over time. 

CVS and Walgreens are currently the two major national competitors in this field. No soda fountain, but lots of general merchandise, including a few aisles of groceries, but also cosmetics, school supplies, candy, and other general merchandise, along with more pharmacy-related goods. And of course an actual pharmacy for your prescription meds. 

Occasionally, you’ll also see the NYC-specific chain Duane Reade in the puzzle, but they’re now part of Walgreens.
